subject: WSJ China: The PLA’s ‘Peace Disease’

REUTERS/CARLOS BARRIA/PRESS POOL   When President Trump stepped off Air Force One in Shenzhen last week for the Asia-Pacific leaders’ summit, Xi Jinping was waiting on the tarmac —a rare gesture recalling Mao Zedong’s reception of Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in 1959. Honor guards from the army, navy, and air force stood at ramrod attention. Jet fighters streaked overhead trailing colored smoke.

   Trump loved it . He has previously praised Chinese military displays as “very, very impressive” and “incredible.” After reviewing an honor guard during a lavish state welcome ceremony in Beijing just six months earlier, he called it “an honor like few have ever seen before.”

   Behind the spectacle is a clear message from Xi: China is strong, the People’s Liberation Army is fearsome, and the man at the top commands it all. But a new report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies offers a sharply different picture of the force behind the pageantry—and it should give both leaders pause.

   The report, titled “ Peace Disease: Is the PLA Battle Ready? ,” draws on interviews with more than 100 officials from the U.S., Australia, India, Japan, the Philippines and Taiwan who have direct experience dealing with Chinese forces in the air and on the sea. Its conclusion: despite China’s impressive arsenal and rapid modernization, the PLA could face significant operational weaknesses in an actual war.

   “Peace disease,” or 和平病 hé píng bìng, is a term Chinese analysts and even Xi himself have used to describe the PLA’s core problem. It hasn’t fought a major war since its border conflict with Vietnam in 1979. And it performed poorly in that one. The PLA has studied other nations’ wars, from the Gulf War to Russia’s war in Ukraine. But studying war and fighting one are very different things.

   Then there’s the purge. According to data compiled by CSIS, some 101 officers who served at the highest levels of China’s military—members of the Central Military Commission, or CMC, theater commanders and their deputies—were purged or went missing between early 2022 and the beginning of 2026.

   As Taylor Fravel, a leading PLA scholar at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, was quoted in the report: “all CMC positions and theater command level positions have experienced a purge,” with roughly 38% of deputy-level positions also affected.

   Corruption and loyalty over competence.   The corruption the purges have uncovered is itself devastating. The CSIS report documents defective weapons, falsified training certifications, fabricated logistics records and poor quality control across the defense industrial base. The question now is whether Xi is replacing the purged officers with combat-effective leaders or political loyalists. Many analysts who study the PLA suspect it’s the latter.

   This matters because, as the CSIS report documents, the PLA’s own internal assessments are candid about its shortcomings. Its officers have cataloged what they call the “five incapables”—commanders who can’t accurately judge a situation, understand their superiors’ intent, make competent operational decisions, deploy troops effectively or deal with the unexpected. The PLA has also identified “two big gaps” between its current state and both its own national security needs and the capabilities of advanced militaries like America’s.

   In a system in which Xi has concentrated more power than any Chinese leader since Mao, subordinates have every incentive to tell him what he wants to hear.

   The CSIS report finds that as party oversight of the military has expanded, commanders face growing uncertainty over which mistakes will be treated as professional errors and which as political failings. That ambiguity, the report says, “naturally encourages consultation, centralized decision-making, and procedural compliance at the expense of rapid battlefield adaptation.”

   It’s the same fear-driven paralysis that has frozen China’s economic policymaking , now extending to the military. As one Chinese military scholar cited in the report put it, there is “insufficient smell of gunpowder” in PLA training.

   That’s the gap Trump should be paying attention to—the one between the PLA’s parade-ground precision and its battlefield readiness. A military that looks formidable on the tarmac yet struggles with the basics of joint operations in wartime poses a specific danger: its commander in chief may not realize how brittle his own force actually is.
